A pangolin is a real, living animal — a mammal — and one of the most extraordinary creatures on Earth.---
What is a Pangolin?

A pangolin is a small-to-medium-sized mammal that is completely covered in hard, overlapping scales, like a walking pinecone or an artichoke. It is the only mammal in the world to have this kind of scaly armour, which makes it completely unique in the animal kingdom.
What Does It Look Like?

Picture a creature with:

  • A long, tapered body and a long tail
  • A small, narrow head with a tiny mouth and no visible ears
  • Short, sturdy legs with powerful curved claws
  • Large, hard scales covering its entire body from head to tail — except for its soft underbelly

The scales are made of keratin, the exact same material your fingernails and hair are made of. They are tough and sharp-edged, and they overlap one another, much like the tiles on a roof.

A pangolin typically grows to about 30 to 100 cm in body length (roughly the size of a house cat to a small dog), depending on the species.
What Does It Eat?

Pangolins are insect-eaters. Their diet consists almost entirely of ants and termites. They dig into ant hills and termite mounds using their powerful claws, and then use their extraordinarily long, sticky tongue — which can be longer than their entire body — to lap up thousands of insects at a time.

Here's something remarkable: pangolins have no teeth at all. Instead, they swallow small stones that sit in their muscular stomach and grind the insects into paste. Nature found its own solution.
How Does It Protect Itself?

When a pangolin feels threatened, it does something very clever — it rolls itself into a tight ball, tucking its head under its tail. In this position, the sharp scales form an almost impenetrable armour on all sides. Even lions and leopards have difficulty breaking through this defence. The name "pangolin" in everyday use has become almost synonymous with this curling-up behaviour.
Where Does It Live?

Pangolins are found in two broad regions of the world:

  • Sub-Saharan Africa (countries like Kenya, South Africa, Zimbabwe)
  • South and Southeast Asia (countries like India, China, Vietnam, Indonesia, the Philippines)

They live in a variety of habitats — forests, grasslands, and savannas. They are nocturnal creatures, meaning they are active mostly at night and spend their days hiding in burrows or hollow trees.

There are eight species of pangolins in total — four found in Africa and four in Asia. They vary somewhat in size and habitat, but all share the same essential features described above.
What Kind of Animal is It, Scientifically?

Pangolins belong to the scientific order Pholidota. Despite looking somewhat like armadillos or anteaters, they are not closely related to either. Their closest relatives are actually carnivores like cats, dogs, and bears — which surprises most people. They are warm-blooded, give birth to live young, and nurse their babies with milk, just like all other mammals.
Why Are Pangolins Important and Endangered?

Pangolins play a critical role in their ecosystems. A single pangolin can eat tens of millions of insects per year, which helps naturally control insect populations and maintain healthy soil.

However, pangolins are in serious danger. They are considered the most trafficked wild mammal on the planet. People illegally hunt and sell them — their scales are falsely believed to have medicinal properties in some cultures, and their meat is considered a delicacy in parts of Asia. All eight species are now threatened or critically endangered.
In Everyday Usage

In most contexts, when someone says the word "pangolin," they simply mean this scaly, ant-eating, curling mammal. It is used both in singular ("a pangolin was spotted near the river") and plural ("pangolins are disappearing fast"). You may also see it used in discussions about wildlife conservation, biodiversity, or illegal animal trade.
The One-Line Summary
A pangolin is a unique, scale-covered, insect-eating mammal that curls into a ball for protection, found in parts of Africa and Asia, and is currently one of the most endangered animals in the world.
PANG-guh-lin
